explanations.explanation: Right at the start, the writer says to "make known His deeds among the nations." (Ps 105:1) That's not news to keep inside one family. The nations are meant to hear it too. I'd stamp it on every cookie if it would fit.

Priests don't show up in this verse at all. The writer says to make His deeds known "among the nations." (Ps 105:1) That's a much bigger crowd than a few people in one room. Keeping this news to a small circle would be like me baking a whole batch and never opening the door to the cookie box.

Elders feel like a natural audience, I get it. But the verse goes wider than that. The writer says to "make known His deeds among the nations." (Ps 105:1) The news is meant to travel a lot farther than one council meeting.

Not quite, friend. The writer says, "Sing to Him, sing praises to Him; tell of all His wonders." (Ps 105:2) All of them, not a highlight reel. Telling only a few would be like stamping one cookie and calling the whole batch done.
That's it. The writer says to "tell of all His wonders." (Ps 105:2) Not a few, ALL. Short version? Friend, I don't even own a short version.
The writer says to "seek His face always." (Ps 105:4) Not once in a while, not when it's convenient, always. That's the kind of habit I like. My ovens never get to feel like it's a day off either.

Feast days are wonderful days, but the verse doesn't put a calendar on it. The writer says to seek His face "always." (Ps 105:4) That means ordinary days too, the quiet ones with nothing special on the schedule. My bakery lights don't only come on for the big batches.

Trouble is a fine time to seek Him, but the writer doesn't stop there. The verse says to "seek His face always." (Ps 105:4) That covers the calm days and the boring Tuesdays too. I don't only check on my oven when I smell smoke.

Yes, the verse says, "Remember the wonders He has done, His marvels…" (Ps 105:5) The memory is about what God has done. The writer is about to walk through exactly that, so there's plenty to remember. My memory only works that well on cookie recipes.

That's not in this verse, friend. The writer says, "Remember the wonders He has done, His marvels…" (Ps 105:5) The spotlight is on what God has done. Reaching for a memory and pulling out a different one is basically my whole afternoon.

A list of kings' names would give any baker a headache. The verse says, "Remember the wonders He has done, His marvels…" (Ps 105:5) Kings do show up later in the psalm, but it's because God rebukes them on behalf of His people (Ps 105:14).

Not quite. The writer says, "His judgments carry throughout the earth." (Ps 105:7) That reaches way past Israel. The writer calls Him "the LORD our God," and His judgments aren't kept in one small corner.

Right, the text says, "His judgments carry throughout the earth." (Ps 105:7) He's the LORD our God, and His judgments reach well past one nation. The earth is a lot of ground. My whole planet is one bakery wide and I still lose things on it.

The verse says, "He remembers His covenant forever…" (Ps 105:8) Forever, friend, with no expiration date stamped on the bottom. The writer adds that it's a word He ordained for a thousand generations. That's a lot of promise to hold onto.
Offerings aren't what this verse says God remembers. It says, "He remembers His covenant forever…" (Ps 105:8) What He holds onto is His own word. He isn't keeping a tally of what people brought.
That's not in this verse. The writer says, "He remembers His covenant forever…" (Ps 105:8) What He remembers is a promise He made. A thousand generations is a very long time to hold one.

The promise says, "I will give you the land of Canaan as the portion of your inheritance." (Ps 105:11) Land, plain and simple. And the writer calls it an inheritance, the kind of thing meant to be passed along.

No throne in this promise. The words are, "I will give you the land of Canaan as the portion of your inheritance." (Ps 105:11) The gift is land, and Canaan is the name on it. A throne would be a lot to keep dusted anyway.

Ships sound fancy, but they're not in this promise. God says, "I will give you the land of Canaan as the portion of your inheritance." (Ps 105:11) It's the land that's promised. Nobody needed a boat to get a portion of dry ground.

The psalm says, "they wandered from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another." (Ps 105:13) Few in number, strangers in the land, and no settled home yet. I think that's a lot of "hi, we're new here" introductions.

No city walls in this verse. It says, "they wandered from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another." (Ps 105:13) They were moving, not building. It's hard to lay bricks when the address keeps changing.

A quiet valley sounds lovely, I'll give you that. But the verse says, "they wandered from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another." (Ps 105:13) They went from place to place, not one spot. No valley got to be home just yet.

Yes, the psalm says, "He let no man oppress them…" (Ps 105:14) They were few, they were strangers, and they were wandering. Even so, no one was allowed to press down on them. That's a lot of protection for a small family on the move.

It's the other way around, friend. The psalm says, "He let no man oppress them…" (Ps 105:14) They had no settled home, and still no one was allowed to press down on them. The writer adds that He rebuked kings for them.

Kings, yes. God rebuked kings on behalf of Abraham's family (Ps 105:14). Kings are the ones with crowns and plenty of say, and they still got told to back off. A small wandering family had God standing up for them.
Priests aren't named in this verse. The psalm says God rebuked kings on behalf of Abraham's family (Ps 105:14). Think about how hard it is to tell a king no. God did it for them.
Elders are a sensible guess, but they're not what the verse says. God rebuked kings on behalf of Abraham's family (Ps 105:14). Kings are people nobody tells no. Here it's God doing the telling.
Not quite. The psalm says Joseph was sold as a slave (Ps 105:17). That's a long way from an honored guest. God sent him ahead of the family, and I think it started out hard.
Right. God sent Joseph ahead of the family, but the psalm says he was sold as a slave (Ps 105:17). A slave, not a guest. The next verses tell us how hard it got (Ps 105:18).

The psalm says he was held "until his prediction came true and the word of the LORD proved him right." (Ps 105:19) The proof came from the LORD's word. In the end, it didn't rest on Joseph's say-so alone.

The psalm doesn't mention that here. It says he was held "until his prediction came true and the word of the LORD proved him right." (Ps 105:19) Whatever anyone else said, this verse credits one thing, the word of the LORD.

I looked up too, old habit, my sky is full of cookie cutter constellations. But this verse has no sign in the sky. It says Joseph's prediction came true and "the word of the LORD proved him right." (Ps 105:19)
The psalm says, "The king sent and released him…" (Ps 105:20) Irons one moment, a message from a king the next. When a king sends for you, things move.
The captain of the guard isn't named in this verse. It says, "The king sent and released him…" (Ps 105:20) The person with the real power here is a king. The order came from the top.

A high priest doesn't appear in this part of the psalm. The verse says, "The king sent and released him…" (Ps 105:20) The one who sends for Joseph is a king. That's who held the power to set him free.
The verse says Joseph gets "to instruct his princes as he pleased and teach his elders wisdom." (Ps 105:22) A man who had been in irons is now the one teaching wisdom to elders. That's some job swap.
No swords in this verse, friend. It says Joseph teaches his elders "wisdom." (Ps 105:22) He was given a place to instruct, and wisdom was the lesson.

Farming would be handy, but it's not what the verse says. It says Joseph would "teach his elders wisdom." (Ps 105:22) I'd have asked him for tips on keeping cookies from burning, but that's not in the text either.
The psalm says, "Israel entered Egypt; Jacob dwelt in the land of Ham." (Ps 105:23) Israel is the name God gave Jacob (Gen 32:28). So the family moves into Egypt.
Assyria is a fair guess for a far-off kingdom, but it's not in this verse. The psalm says, "Israel entered Egypt; Jacob dwelt in the land of Ham." (Ps 105:23) Egypt is where the family goes.
Moab doesn't show up here. The verse says, "Israel entered Egypt; Jacob dwelt in the land of Ham." (Ps 105:23) The family's new home is Egypt, and the writer says Jacob dwelt there.
The psalm says, "the LORD made His people very fruitful, more numerous than their foes…" (Ps 105:24) Earlier they were "few in number, few indeed." (Ps 105:12) That's a big turnaround for one family.
Few was how they started out (Ps 105:12), but that's not where it stays. The verse says, "the LORD made His people very fruitful…" (Ps 105:24) Nothing in it says they were hidden.
Nothing here about sending them back. The verse says the LORD made His people "very fruitful." (Ps 105:24) They've just entered Egypt, and the next thing the psalm tells us is that they grow.
Yes, the psalm says the LORD made His people "more numerous than their foes." (Ps 105:24) This is the same family that was "few in number, few indeed." (Ps 105:12) From a handful to a crowd.

It's actually true, friend. The psalm says the LORD made His people "more numerous than their foes." (Ps 105:24) They started out "few in number, few indeed." (Ps 105:12) That's quite the growth spurt.

explanations.answer: God turned them to hate His people
explanations.explanation: The psalm says, "whose hearts He turned to hate His people, to conspire against His servants." (Ps 105:25) That's a heavy line. I'm keeping the text's own words and not adding a reason it doesn't give.

explanations.answer: God softened them toward His people
explanations.explanation: It's the opposite, friend. The psalm says, "whose hearts He turned to hate His people, to conspire against His servants." (Ps 105:25) This is a heavy part of the song. I'll leave the words as the writer gave them.

explanations.answer: God made them forget His people
explanations.explanation: Forgetting isn't what the psalm says. It says, "whose hearts He turned to hate His people, to conspire against His servants." (Ps 105:25) This is a heavy line. It's best to read it just as it stands.

The psalm says, "They performed His miraculous signs among them, and wonders in the land of Ham." (Ps 105:27) Notice they're His signs, not their own. God sent Moses and Aaron (Ps 105:26), and these are the things they did there.

explanations.answer: Build store cities for the king
explanations.explanation: No building crew here. The psalm says God sent Moses and Aaron (Ps 105:26), and "They performed His miraculous signs among them, and wonders in the land of Ham." (Ps 105:27) They were sent to do His signs. A king's construction project isn't in this verse.

No recruiting table in this psalm. It says Moses and Aaron "performed His miraculous signs among them, and wonders in the land of Ham." (Ps 105:27) Two men sent by God, doing His signs. That's the whole job description.
The psalm says, "He turned their waters to blood and caused their fish to die." (Ps 105:29) The water changes and the fish die. Tough day for the whole river crowd.
Bigger fish would be a nice twist, but that's not what happens. The psalm says, "He turned their waters to blood and caused their fish to die." (Ps 105:29) The fish die. Nothing about growing.

Leaping ashore would make quite a scene, but the verse doesn't say that. It says, "He turned their waters to blood and caused their fish to die." (Ps 105:29) The frogs don't show up until the next verse (Ps 105:30), so they've got that part covered.

Yes, the psalm says, "He struck their vines and fig trees and shattered the trees of their country." (Ps 105:33) Vines, fig trees and the trees of the country all took the hit. That comes right after the hail and lightning (Ps 105:32).

It's actually true, friend. The psalm says, "He struck their vines and fig trees and shattered the trees of their country." (Ps 105:33) It follows the hail and lightning of the verse before (Ps 105:32). The vines and the fig trees were hit.

The psalm says, "They devoured every plant in their land and consumed the produce of their soil." (Ps 105:35) Every plant. I've watched a cookie box empty at a family get-together in minutes, but this is a whole different level.

Only the king's gardens would be an easier read, but the verse is bigger than that. It says, "They devoured every plant in their land and consumed the produce of their soil." (Ps 105:35) The whole land is in view.

explanations.answer: Only the fields by the river
explanations.explanation: The river fields aren't singled out here. The psalm says, "They devoured every plant in their land and consumed the produce of their soil." (Ps 105:35) Every plant in the land is the claim. That leaves no one corner untouched.
Not at all, friend. The psalm says, "He brought Israel out with silver and gold, and none among His tribes stumbled." (Ps 105:37) They left with silver and gold. Pockets full and nobody stumbling.

That's it. The psalm says, "He brought Israel out with silver and gold, and none among His tribes stumbled." (Ps 105:37) They didn't leave with nothing in their hands. Silver, gold, and nobody tripping on the way out.
The psalm says, "Egypt was glad when they departed, for the dread of Israel had fallen on them." (Ps 105:38) The writer even gives the reason. The dread of Israel had fallen on them.

Furious is a fair guess after everything that happened. But the psalm says, "Egypt was glad when they departed, for the dread of Israel had fallen on them." (Ps 105:38) Glad is the word the text uses.

No tearful goodbyes here. The psalm says, "Egypt was glad when they departed, for the dread of Israel had fallen on them." (Ps 105:38) Nobody threw a farewell party and nobody wrote a card. Egypt was glad.
The psalm says, "He spread a cloud as a covering and a fire to light up the night." (Ps 105:39) A cloud for cover and a fire for the dark. Built-in shade and a built-in porch light.

A tent and a lamp make a sensible pair, but they're not what the verse says. It says, "He spread a cloud as a covering and a fire to light up the night." (Ps 105:39) The covering is a cloud and the light is a fire.

A wall and a tower would suit a place with a gate, but that's not this verse. The psalm says, "He spread a cloud as a covering and a fire to light up the night." (Ps 105:39) A cloud and a fire are what He gave them.
The psalm says, "He opened a rock, and water gushed out; it flowed like a river in the desert." (Ps 105:41) Water out of a rock, friend. I've cracked plenty of cookies and never once got a river.
A well is a sensible guess for water. But this verse has a rock. The psalm says, "He opened a rock, and water gushed out; it flowed like a river in the desert." (Ps 105:41)

A cistern holds water, so I see where you're coming from. But the verse says, "He opened a rock, and water gushed out; it flowed like a river in the desert." (Ps 105:41) The water came out of a rock, and it flowed like a river.

explanations.answer: He remembered His promise to Abraham
explanations.explanation: The writer says, "For He remembered His holy promise to Abraham His servant." (Ps 105:42) The reason named is His promise. It circles right back to the covenant from the start of the song (Ps 105:8-9).
The psalm gives a different reason. It says, "For He remembered His holy promise to Abraham His servant." (Ps 105:42) The reason named is His promise. Earning isn't mentioned.

The psalm doesn't mention Egypt insulting His name. It says, "For He remembered His holy promise to Abraham His servant." (Ps 105:42) The reason the writer gives is that promise. I'll leave the insult-keeping to people with more free time.

explanations.answer: So they would keep His laws
explanations.explanation: The psalm says the lands were given "that they might keep His statutes and obey His laws. Hallelujah!" (Ps 105:45) That's the purpose the writer names. And then the song ends with a shout of praise.

explanations.answer: So they would build an army
explanations.explanation: No army in this verse. The psalm says the lands were given "that they might keep His statutes and obey His laws. Hallelujah!" (Ps 105:45) Keeping His statutes and laws is the purpose the writer names.

explanations.answer: So they would rule over Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt isn't named in this purpose. The psalm says the lands were given "that they might keep His statutes and obey His laws. Hallelujah!" (Ps 105:45) The song ends on His statutes and laws, with a Hallelujah.
